title: Senior's toolkit: exploring a database from the terminal
summary: sqlite3 and psql commands for finding your way around tables, plus the SELECT habits that keep exploration cheap and correct.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: exploring a database from the terminal
steps.body: Most SQL at work starts with an unfamiliar database and a question. Experienced people open a client, list the tables, read the schema and look at a few rows before writing the real query.

toolkit.what: Open a SQLite database in the command-line shell, or run one query and exit.
flags: open without any risk of changing the file
print results as a bordered table
run this one statement and exit

toolkit.what: sqlite3 dot commands, typed at the `sqlite>` prompt. They are not SQL, so they take no semicolon.
flags: show the CREATE statement, with columns, keys and indexes
show column names in `column` or `csv` mode

toolkit.what: The PostgreSQL command-line client. Connect with a URL or with `-h -U -d`.
flags: stop at the first error (always use it with -f)

toolkit.what: psql meta-commands for finding your way around (they start with a backslash).
flags: columns, types, defaults, indexes, constraints and size of a table
show wide rows one field per line when they do not fit

toolkit.what: Always cap exploratory queries, and sort so the rows you see mean something. SQL Server spells it `TOP 20` or `OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY`.
flags: without it, row order is not guaranteed
put NULLs at the end (PostgreSQL, SQLite 3.30+)
toolkit.example: SELECT id, title, published FROM books ORDER BY published DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 20;

toolkit.what: The NULL tools you use every week. `=` and `<>` are never true when one side is NULL; these make the intent explicit.
flags: the first value that is not NULL
NULL when a equals b (e.g. avoid dividing by 0)
a NULL-safe `<>` (PostgreSQL, SQL Server 2022, SQLite 3.39+; older SQLite: `IS NOT`)

steps.prompt: sqlite3 dot command or psql meta-command?
There are 55 books that are not discontinued, but this query returns 40. Fifteen books have `discontinued` set to NULL (never filled in). Which query returns all 55?
steps.code: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM books WHERE discontinued <> 1;
options: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM books WHERE NOT discontinued = 1;`
steps.explain: `NULL <> 1` is UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE, so the 15 NULL rows vanish. `!=` and `NOT ... =` behave the same. `COALESCE` (or `IS DISTINCT FROM 1`) treats NULL as "not discontinued" on purpose.

steps.prompt: Look at five rows of the production copy without any risk of changing it.
steps.explain: `-readonly` opens the file read-only, so a slip of the keyboard cannot change it. SQLite uses `LIMIT`; `TOP` is SQL Server.

steps.prompt: Match each command to the moment you use it.
pairs: a row has 30 columns and wraps into an unreadable mess
you need the column types and indexes of a Postgres table
running a script that must stop if one statement fails
you need the CREATE statement of a SQLite table
peeking at a table that might have millions of rows

steps.prompt: You run `psql -f backfill.sql` against staging. Statement 3 of 10 fails with a typo, and psql keeps going. Why is that dangerous, and what prevents it?
options: Statements 4 to 10 run on top of a half-done change; `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` makes psql stop at the first error
It is not dangerous: psql rolls back the whole file on any error
psql stops by default; the typo must have been in a comment
Use `\x auto` so errors are easier to read
steps.explain: By default psql reports the error and runs the next statement. With `ON_ERROR_STOP=1` it exits with a non-zero code, which also makes a CI job fail as it should.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Before writing a query against a database you do not know, list the tables, read the schema of the ones you need and look at a few rows with `LIMIT`. When a count looks wrong, ask first whether NULLs are being dropped by `=` or `<>`.
